title: Summer cotton stole
subtitle: A long open-mesh rectangle in fingering-weight cotton, worked in a ch-1 skip-1 dc grid
excerpt: This rectangular stole uses a ch-1, skip-1, dc mesh pattern on a 3.5 mm hook with fingering or sport-weight cotton. The open grid creates a light, airy fabric that sits flat without blocking. Finished size is approximately 200 cm long by 50 cm wide, giving enough length to wrap, drape, or loop over the shoulders.

glossaryTerms.definition: A crochet structure made by alternating double crochet stitches with chain-1 spaces, each new dc worked into the ch-1 space of the previous row rather than into a stitch. The result is an open grid of regular square holes.

content.text: This stole works a ch-1, skip-1, dc repeat across a long rectangle, producing an open grid fabric that is airy enough for warm weather but structured enough to hold a drape. The yarn is fingering or sport-weight cotton on a 3.5 mm hook. At 200 cm by 50 cm the finished piece wraps as a stole, folds as a scarf, or drapes across both shoulders.
The
mesh pattern

repeats over an even number of foundation chains. On every row each dc sits above a ch-1 space from the previous row, not above a stitch, so the pattern stays consistent and the grid aligns naturally.

attrs.title: Materials
attrs.body: Approximately 300 g fingering or sport-weight cotton yarn. A 3.5 mm crochet hook (US E/4). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Tape measure.

content.text: Gauge

14 mesh repeats (dc, ch 1) x 14 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering-weight cotton with a 3.5 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a 15 x 15 cm swatch in the mesh pattern, count the central 10 cm, and adjust the hook size if needed before starting the foundation chain.
Stitches used
chain (ch): UK and US shared.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
Pattern

The stole is worked flat along its length, so the foundation chain is the short end (50 cm width) and the rows build the 200 cm length. This orientation means you work fewer, longer rows rather than many short ones, which keeps the work manageable on the hook.
Foundation chain
Ch 143. (This gives 71 mesh repeats across 50 cm of width.)
Row 1 (right side)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the 2nd ch from hook. *Ch 1, skip 1 ch, 1 dc in the next ch*; repeat from * to * to end. Turn. (72 dc, 71 ch-1 spaces)
Row 2
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the first dc. *Ch 1, 1 dc in the next ch-1 space*; repeat from * to * to last dc. 1 dc in the last dc. Turn. (72 dc, 70 ch-1 spaces)
Rows 3 onwards

Repeat row 2 on every subsequent row. The pattern is: ch 1 (does not count as stitch), 1 dc in the first dc, *ch 1, 1 dc in next ch-1 space*, repeat to last dc, 1 dc in last dc. Turn. (72 dc, 70 ch-1 spaces each row)
Continue to approximately row 280
Continue row 2 pattern until the piece measures 200 cm from the foundation chain edge, measured flat. At 14 rows per 10 cm this is approximately 280 rows in total. Fasten off.
Finishing

Fasten off and weave in both ends. Thread the tail through several stitches along the selvedge, pulling gently to secure. Cotton does not felt so ends must be woven in a minimum of 5 cm. The mesh fabric sits flat without blocking; if the edges curl, lightly spray and pin to shape while damp.
Care
Machine-wash at 30 degrees on a gentle cycle, or handwash in cool water. Cotton can be tumble-dried on a low setting. Lay flat to dry for best results.
What to try next

Work the same mesh pattern in linen yarn for a crisper, stiffer drape that softens with washing. Alternate two colours every two rows to create a subtle striped mesh. A narrow double-crochet border worked around all four edges gives clean selvedges and stops the corners rolling.
